title: Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt, Notion

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 64%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on coding agents (Claude, Cursor in Notion) and the IDE/PR loop, with techniques for understanding and reviewing agent-written code. Coding assistants (Claude, Cursor) are integrated into Notion as a developer platform for building code with agents. The techniques are applied during the development and code review phase. The talk is accessible but assumes familiarity with coding agents and software engineering workflows. This is a conference talk at the AI Engineer conference. All evidence anchors are directly stated in the transcript.

summary: Geoffrey Litt, a design engineer at Notion, argues that understanding code remains essential even as AI agents write more of it. He challenges the common view that understanding is primarily for correctness verification, proposing instead that understanding enables active creative participation across iterative development loops. Without it, you accumulate 'cognitive debt'—degraded understanding that eventually blocks meaningful participation. Drawing from education and cognitive science, Litt shares three techniques. The first is explainer docs generated by his 'explainerif' skill, featuring background context first, intuition before details, interactive figures via Notion's HTML blocks, and literate code diffs. He adds spaced-repetition quizzes (inspired by Andy Matuschak) to verify genuine comprehension, refusing to send agent-written code for team review until he passes the quiz—acting as a 'speed regulator.' The second technique is microworlds, inspired by educator Seymour Papert's vision of 'Mathland'—environments where you learn by inhabiting them. Litt demonstrates with a Prolog interpreter debugger that visualizes internal state step-by-step, and a personal website migration turned into a step-by-step 'video game.' The key insight: agents can write code to help us understand code, building ephemeral simulations rather than shipping software. The third technique is shared spaces. Litt notes that team understanding is often the real challenge. Notion explores multiplayer chat threads between humans and agents, and collaborative documents where teammates can discuss agent-generated plans together. Notion launched coding agents (Claude and Cursor) in Notion the prior week. Litt closes by connecting his thesis to Alan Kay's 50-year-old essay envisioning computers as tools to level up humans. He argues that AI-generated ephemeral UIs, dynamic simulations, and playgrounds are not new ideas but the original goal of computing. With the right tools and mindset, AI can put us more deeply in loops than ever before, empowering rather than removing humans.

sections.title: Opening and the Hot Take
sections.summary: Litt introduces himself as a design engineer at Notion and poses the provocative question that it's still important for people to understand how code works, polling the audience for agreement and disagreement.

sections.title: Why Understanding Matters: Verification vs. Participation
sections.summary: Litt challenges the common model that understanding is for correctness verification, arguing agents are improving at self-verification. The deeper reason is understanding to participate—each loop changes you and builds conceptual structures for creative leaps in future iterations.

sections.title: Cognitive Debt
sections.summary: Introduces 'cognitive debt' (popularized by Margaret... and Simon Willison), analogous to technical debt. You can get away with degraded understanding for a while, but eventually you can no longer participate.

sections.title: Education as Inspiration
sections.summary: Litt reframes the 'how' question by asking how humans understand in general, turning to the field of education for proven techniques adapted to AI agent workflows. Previews three techniques.

sections.title: Technique 1: Explanations and Explainer Docs
sections.summary: Details his 'explainerif' skill producing explainer docs with four principles: background context first, intuition before details, interactive figures (using Notion's new HTML blocks), and literate code diffs with prose. Demonstrates with a Zen garden game example.

sections.title: Quizzes to Verify Understanding
sections.summary: Addresses the problem that reading is unreliable—people fool themselves. Inspired by Andy Matuschak's spaced-repetition quizzes, Litt adds five-question quizzes to explainer docs and won't send code for review until he passes. Acts as a 'speed regulator.' Shares the Explain Diff skill via QR code in two versions (HTML and Notion output).

sections.title: Technique 2: Microworlds
sections.summary: Inspired by Seymour Papert's Mathland concept and turtle robot—kids learn math by inhabiting an environment. Litt demonstrates with a Prolog interpreter microworld: an ephemeral debugger UI visualizing internal state step-by-step with timeline scrubbing and commenting, and a personal website migration turned into a step-by-step 'video game' showing file movements. Key takeaway: agents can write code to help us understand code.

sections.title: Technique 3: Shared Spaces
sections.summary: Extends understanding from solo to team. Notion explores multiplayer chat threads where multiple humans and agents communicate in shared space, and collaborative documents where teammates discuss agent-generated plans. Notion launched coding agents (Claude and Cursor) in Notion the prior week; Litt's team builds code in Notion for the shared-space benefits.

sections.title: Closing: Alan Kay and the Original Vision
sections.summary: Connects the thesis to Alan Kay's 50-year-old essay 'A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages,' which envisioned kids modifying code as they play to learn. Kay's vision was computers leveling up humans, not replacing them. Litt argues AI-generated ephemeral UIs and simulations are the original goal resurgent. With right tools and mindset, AI can put us more deeply in loops, empowering us to understand better than ever.
